title: US Universities Issue Urgent Advisory as DHS Ends Open-Ended Student Visas
excerpt: Several American universities are advising international students currently abroad to return before September 15, when new DHS rules replace the flexible "Duration of Status" system with a hard four-year cap on F-1 visa stays.
body:
• DHS final rule published July 16 replaces the decades-old "Duration of Status" framework with a four-year cap on F-1 and J-1 visa stays, effective September 15, 2026.
  • Post-graduation grace period cut from 60 to 30 days; extensions now require USCIS application with biometrics and background checks.
  • Indian students — the largest international cohort in the US with over 363,000 enrolled — face acute uncertainty, especially those in PhD programmes averaging 5.6 years.
  • India's MEA says it is in contact with Washington and will advocate for genuine students affected by the transition.

American universities are scrambling to prepare international students for one of the most sweeping immigration changes in decades. The US Department of Homeland Security published a final rule on July 16 that abolishes the long-standing "Duration of Status" framework for F-1 student visas, replacing it with a fixed four-year cap on stays. The rule takes effect on September 15, 2026.

Several universities have already advised international students currently outside the country to return before the September 15 deadline to avoid complications during the transition, according to Outlook Traveller. The University of Washington said it is analysing the more than 500-page document and will reach out to affected students once that review is complete.

What Changes on September 15

For nearly five decades, international students on F-1 and J-1 visas could remain in the US for as long as they were enrolled and making normal academic progress — a system known as "Duration of Status." Under the new rule, students will receive a fixed admission period capped at four years. Those needing more time must apply for an Extension of Stay through US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS), a process involving biometric verification, background checks, and additional scrutiny.

The post-graduation grace period has been halved — from 60 days to 30. Students will have just one month after completing their programme to leave, transfer institutions, change visa status, or begin steps toward Optional Practical Training (OPT). The rule also restricts switching academic programmes, changing majors, or transferring between institutions, shifting authority from universities to federal immigration agencies.

"The duration of status rule that has been proposed is going to fundamentally change the flexibility that students have had to apply for Optional Practical Training and Curricular Practical Training."

— Danielle Goldman, Co-founder and CEO, Build

Why PhD Students Face the Biggest Risk

The four-year cap poses a particular challenge for doctoral candidates. On average, it takes 5.6 years to complete a PhD in science or engineering in the United States, according to Nature. With roughly 488,000 international graduate students enrolled in the 2024–25 academic year, researchers warn the new framework could hollow out America's research pipeline.

"For decades, international students have been encouraged to come and study in the United States. These restrictions mark the dissolution of the dream of becoming a leading US innovator and scientist."

— Bennett Goldberg, Physicist, Northwestern University

The rule also prohibits graduate students on F-1 visas from switching programmes or institutions — a restriction that could trap students in programmes that are no longer a good fit.

Impact on Indian Students

India sends the largest contingent of international students to the United States. According to the Open Doors 2025 report, 363,019 Indian students were enrolled at American institutions in the 2024–25 academic year, accounting for nearly 31 percent of all international students.

New Delhi has signalled it is monitoring the situation. MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said at a press briefing that India is in contact with Washington and will take up difficulties faced by genuine students. "As and when there are issues of difficulties, which are brought to our attention, in regard to genuine travellers and students, we take up those issues with the US side so as to minimise the difficulties that our people face," he said.

Immigration experts have flagged a knock-on effect on OPT. While the programme itself remains unchanged, students must now ensure their underlying F-1 admission stays valid throughout their OPT period — a complication that could catch graduates off guard if their fixed admission expires while they are working.

What's Next

Current students already in the US under the old D/S system will automatically transition to the new framework, with their authorised stay capped at four years from the effective date. Students arriving after September 15 will receive date-specific admission documents from the outset.

Higher education groups including the Association of American Universities have formally opposed the rule. NAFSA, the association of international educators, called the changes "a dangerous overreach by government into academia" that would force students "into a sea of administrative delays at best, and at worst, into unlawful presence status."

For Indian students weighing fall admissions or mid-programme travel plans, the advice from universities and immigration attorneys is consistent: if you are outside the US, return before September 15.
